parole.testo: Via Low German Appelsina, from Dutch appelsina (cp. appelsien, for which now usually sinaasappel). So named because of their introduction to Europe from China (Latin Sīna).

Formally from Low German Düker, from Middle Low German düker (“diver”, also “culvert”?). Doublet of Taucher ("diver"). The sense “culvert” may be a loan translation of Dutch duiker. At least its adoption into standard German was probably reinforced by Dutch.

From Low Franconian and Low German dialects along the Dutch border, which it entered (before 1930) from Dutch fiets, perhaps partly through Dutch Low Saxon fietse. Further origin uncertain. In an alternative theory, the direction of derivation went the other way. See the Dutch etymology.
Borrowed from Low German, from Dutch kous (“stocking”). Cognate with Danish kovs.

parole.significato: to list (to lean towards the sides or rotate around the long axis, of ships or similar vessels)
parole.testo: According to Duden, borrowed from Low German krengen, in turn from Dutch krengen. Whether borrowed or inherited, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *krangijaną.

From Low German püükfien, tautological compound of püük + fien, both roughly “excellent, fine, clean, honest”. The former is a borrowing from Dutch puik, from Middle Dutch puuc, from Old Dutch *puiken, from Proto-West Germanic *pūka, *pūga, from Pre-Germanic *pūkk, of uncertain origin, possibly Prot
Borrowed from Low German or Dutch potsig (“funny, cute”), which belongs to Old French bocer.; related to Butz (“goblin”).
Borrowed from Low German Rabauke, diminutive of Rabau (“rogue, scoundrel”), from Dutch rabauw, from Middle Dutch rabaut, from Old French ribaut. See ribald
From Low German Rüümte, from Middle Low German rūmte; perhaps also influenced by cognate Dutch ruimte. Analysable as raum (“wide”) + -te; compare geräumig. Also cognate with English roomth.

parole.significato: dock worker who loads and unloads ships, lumper
parole.testo: 19th century, from Low German Schauer, from Dutch sjouwer, derived from sjouwen, from West Frisian sjouwe.
From Low German sorren, *zorren, perhaps from Dutch tsorren, older variant of sjorren. Further origin uncertain.
